By the Nash–Williams–Tutte theorem, $\tau(G)<k$ implies a vertex partition $\mathcal P$ into $r$ parts with $e(\mathcal P)\le k(r-1)-1$. Since $G$ is $(k+1)$-edge-connected, every part $V_i$ satisfies $d(V_i)\ge k+1$, so $2e(\mathcal P)=\sum d(V_i)\ge r(k+1)$. Combining these gives $r(k+1)\le 2k(r-1)-2$, which forces $r\ge k+1$ for $k\ge 3$.

To maximize the spectral radius we concentrate edges inside one part. Taking $r=k+1$ with one part $A$ of size $n-k$ and $k$ singletons, the edge-count bound becomes $e(\mathcal P)\le k^2-1$. Moving any edge inside $A$ increases the spectral radius (Perron–Frobenius edge-attachment), so $A$ must be a clique. The $k$ remaining vertices contribute at most $e(\mathcal P)=k^2-1$ edges in total (joining them to $A$ and among themselves), and the $(k+1)$-edge-connectivity condition is satisfied precisely when these $k^2-1$ edges are placed so that each singleton has degree at least $k+1$—feasible for $n\ge 3k+2$.

Hence the unique extremal graph $F_{n,k}$ consists of a clique on $n-k$ vertices plus exactly $k^2-1$ further edges, yielding

\[
|E(F_{n,k})|=\binom{n-k}{2}+k^2-1.
\]

\boxed{\binom{n-k}{2} + k^2 - 1}
